title: Starting a Hospice Program in New Hampshire: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

html:
Introduction

Starting a Hospice Program in New Hampshire represents a meaningful opportunity to serve individuals requiring end-of-life care, including comfort, pain management, and psychosocial support, while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and funding are administered by the New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and the state’s Medicaid program.

With minimal wait times and a strong preference for a home-based care model, New Hampshire offers a market with established providers in urban centers but significant opportunities in rural areas and specialized niches for providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. Reimbursement rates, such as the Routine Home Care Medicaid rate of $211.61 per day and a 4.1% Medicare rate increase in FY2023, signal a stable financial environment for qualified agencies.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Hospice Program in New Hampshire, from understanding state and federal regulations and licensing to staffing your interdisciplinary team, managing reimbursement, and preparing for inspections.

Table of Contents

  • Understand New Hampshire’s Hospice Program Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand New Hampshire’s Hospice Program Regulations

New Hampshire regulates Hospice Programs through the New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), which is responsible for overseeing patient care standards, staffing qualifications, emergency preparedness, patient rights, and quality assurance. Because hospice is a federally defined benefit, providers serving Medicare or Medicaid populations must also comply with the rigorous Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Conditions of Participation (CoPs) and the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA).

The regulatory framework emphasizes ensuring quality of life, patient-centered care, and comprehensive interdisciplinary support at the end of life. This includes a focus on robust care planning, documented patient and family involvement, effective pain and symptom management, and bereavement support. Licenses typically require renewal every 1 to 2 years, contingent on successful surveys and adherence to state rules.

Navigating the dual requirements of DHHS and CMS is the most critical part of the startup process. Success depends on building your operational framework around these rules from day one.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

New Hampshire supports multiple hospice service models, primarily defined by the four levels of care mandated by Medicare. Each has different staffing, documentation, and reimbursement requirements:

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): The most common level of care, where services are provided in the patient’s residence, whether it’s a private home, assisted living facility, or nursing home. This aligns with New Hampshire’s strong preference for home-based models.
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): Provided during periods of crisis to manage acute medical symptoms. It involves 8 to 24 hours of nursing care per day to keep the patient at home.
  • General Inpatient Care (GIP): For pain or symptom management that cannot be handled in another setting. This care is provided in a Medicare-certified hospital, hospice inpatient facility, or skilled nursing facility.
  • Inpatient Respite Care: Short-term inpatient care provided to the patient to relieve their family or other caregivers. It is limited to five consecutive days at a time.

Beyond these core levels, strategic providers can find success by developing specialized service lines. The New Hampshire market has identified needs for pediatric hospice, dementia-specific care programs, rural mobile units, and palliative care integration. Focusing on one of these niches can differentiate your agency and address unmet community needs.

Program size is measured by Average Daily Census (ADC). A new agency might start by targeting an ADC of 15-25 patients and scale from there. Demand is strongest in urban centers like Manchester, Nashua, and the Merrimack Valley, which also have the highest provider concentration. In contrast, rural areas may offer significant entry opportunities with less competition, though they require a robust plan for managing travel time and staff logistics.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can serve patients, you must establish a formal business entity and secure the necessary licenses. Providers typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or a Corporation (S-Corp or C-Corp) due to the liability protection these structures offer.

You must:

  • Register your business with the New Hampshire Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (malpractice), and workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a comprehensive licensing application to the New Hampshire DHHS. This application will require detailed information about your agency’s ownership, governing body, key personnel, financial solvency, and draft policies and procedures.

Licensing timelines, including the crucial Medicare certification process, generally range from 9 to 18 months. This timeframe is highly dependent on your team’s readiness, the completeness of your application, and your ability to pass the initial licensure and certification surveys. Delays are common, so meticulous preparation is essential.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A detailed business plan is your roadmap for financial success and a requirement for securing funding. Startup costs for a hospice in New Hampshire typically range from $200,000 to $600,000. This capital covers licensing and legal fees, office space and equipment, an Electronic Medical Record (EMR) system, initial payroll before revenue begins, and marketing.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by staffing, which represents 55-65% of total costs. This reflects the interdisciplinary team model required by CMS. Your financial projections must be built around the per-diem reimbursement model.

Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges include:

  • Medicaid Routine Home Care: $211.61 per day (as a baseline example).
  • Medicare Rates: Medicare is the primary payer for over 90% of hospice care. Rates are set annually by CMS, with a 4.1% increase for FY2023, and vary by level of care and geographic location.

Providers operating at a target utilization, often an Average Daily Census (ADC) of 20-30 patients to reach break-even, can generally achieve around 8% Medicare profit margins. Your business plan must include detailed projections showing the path to a sustainable ADC and profitability, which often takes 12-18 months.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Given the home-based care model prevalent in New Hampshire, your primary physical location will be an administrative office, not a large inpatient facility. However, this office must meet specific state and federal requirements.

Facility and office requirements include:

  • HIPAA-compliant storage for physical patient records and business documents.
  • A secure, professional space for your administrative and clinical leadership team.
  • A conference room large enough to hold mandatory Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) meetings.
  • Secure storage for medical supplies and equipment.
  • Accessibility for staff and any visitors, complying with ADA standards.
  • Contracts with inpatient facilities (hospitals or SNFs) if you plan to offer General Inpatient or Respite care.

Location selection should consider proximity to major referral sources like hospitals, zoning regulations, and accessibility for your workforce. Choosing a central location within your desired service area can help minimize staff travel time and improve operational efficiency.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

The heart of any hospice is its Interdisciplinary Group (IDG), a team of professionals who work together to create and manage each patient’s plan of care. This team is mandated by CMS, and having qualified individuals in these roles is a prerequisite for licensure.

Required roles typically include:

  • Medical Director: A physician who provides clinical oversight and direction for the IDG.
  • Administrator/Director of Nursing: An RN responsible for the day-to-day operations and clinical management of the agency.
  • Registered Nurse (RN) Case Managers: Manage a caseload of patients, conducting assessments and coordinating care.
  • Medical Social Worker (MSW): Provides psychosocial support to patients and families and connects them with community resources.
  • Spiritual Counselor/Chaplain: Offers spiritual support aligned with the patient’s and family’s beliefs.
  • Hospice Aides: Provide personal care to patients under the supervision of an RN.
  • Volunteer Coordinator: Manages the required hospice volunteer program.

Training is a major focus of regulatory surveys. All staff must receive comprehensive orientation and ongoing education. Training requirements include hospice philosophy, pain and symptom management, patient rights, infection control, emergency procedures, and discipline-specific skills. Documentation of all training is mandatory.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Your agency cannot operate without a comprehensive set of written policies and procedures that serve as the rulebook for your staff and the proof of your compliance for regulators. New Hampshire and CMS require written policies covering all aspects of clinical and administrative operations.

Key policy requirements include:

  • Patient Rights and Responsibilities
  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Care Planning Process (including the IDG’s role and frequency of meetings)
  • Pain and Symptom Management Protocols
  • Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI) Program
  • Infection Control and Prevention
  • Emergency Preparedness Plan
  • Volunteer Program Management
  • Bereavement Support Services

Individual care plans are the central document in hospice care. They must be developed by the IDG in collaboration with the patient and family within days of admission. These plans must be dynamic, reviewed at least every 15 days, and meticulously documented in your EMR to reflect the patient’s changing needs and goals.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Hospice services are not marketed directly to consumers through traditional advertising. Instead, success is built on developing trust and strong professional relationships with referral sources within the healthcare community.

Referrals for hospice care in New Hampshire typically come from:

  • Hospital discharge planners and case managers
  • Physicians (especially oncologists, cardiologists, pulmonologists, and primary care doctors)
  • Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs)
  • Assisted Living Facilities
  • Home Health Agencies

Your marketing efforts should focus on educating these professionals about your agency’s unique strengths, such as expertise in dementia care, rapid response times, or your commitment to serving rural communities. Successful providers focus on demonstrating compliance, clinical excellence, responsiveness, and clear communication rather than on flashy brochures. Building a reputation as a reliable partner is the most effective marketing strategy.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Achieving licensure is the start, not the end, of your compliance journey. Your hospice will be subject to ongoing oversight and unannounced inspections.

Oversight includes surveys conducted by the New Hampshire DHHS for state licensure and either DHHS surveyors on behalf of CMS or an accrediting organization like the Community Health Accreditation Partner (CHAP) or The Joint Commission for Medicare certification. Inspections are rigorous and focus on direct patient observation, clinical record reviews, and staff interviews.

Common deficiencies often relate to:

  • Incomplete or outdated patient care plans
  • Failure to hold IDG meetings every 15 days
  • Insufficient supervision of hospice aides
  • Errors in medication management documentation
  • Gaps in the Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI) program

Maintaining a state of continuous survey readiness is the only way to ensure compliance. This requires regular internal audits, ongoing staff training, and a robust quality improvement program that actively identifies and corrects potential issues before a surveyor finds them.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

  • How long does it take to open a Hospice Program in New Hampshire?

It typically takes 9 to 18 months to open a hospice. This includes time for business registration, writing a business plan, completing the state license application, and undergoing the critical Medicare certification process, which involves an extensive application and an initial survey.

  • What licenses are required?

You need a Hospice Program license issued by the New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). To receive payment from Medicare, you must also become Medicare Certified, a separate process that ensures you meet federal Conditions of Participation (CoPs).

  • What reimbursement is available?

Reimbursement is primarily from Medicare Part A, which pays a per diem (daily) rate. Rates vary based on the level of care provided (Routine, Continuous, Inpatient, or Respite). New Hampshire Medicaid also covers hospice services, with the Routine Home Care rate at $211.61 per day, providing a useful financial benchmark.

Conclusion

Starting a Hospice Program in New Hampshire is a complex but deeply rewarding venture. It requires careful planning, a deep understanding of state and federal regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. The market offers clear opportunities for providers who can deliver high-quality, compassionate care, particularly in underserved rural areas or specialized clinical niches.

Providers who invest in a foundation of compliance, hire and train a dedicated interdisciplinary team, and build strong relationships within the local healthcare community are positioned for long-term success and sustainability. By focusing on patient-centered care and continuous quality improvement, you can build an agency that makes a profound difference in the lives of patients and families across the Granite State.
